reasoning: The study generated original research data: PET imaging data (11C-PBR28, 18F-flortaucipir), MRI cortical thickness measures, neuropsychological test results, and neuropathology findings from patients and healthy controls recruited and scanned specifically for this study. This constitutes clear data generation (D1). For software, the paper only used existing established tools (Freesurfer, PMOD, SPM12, MATLAB curve fitting toolbox, IBM SPSS) for processing/analysis without claiming to have created or significantly extended any software - these are used as utilities for standard analysis pipelines (S2).

The paper uses existing research software (SNANA for simulations, SALT2 fitter, emcee MCMC sampler, CosmoMC, PSNID classifier) without claiming to have created a new software package of its own (BEAMS is implemented as a methodology using these tools, and while code is made available on GitHub, this is presented as an implementation/analysis script rather than a significantly new, generically reusable software package - it's used to apply an established method, KBH07's BEAMS, to existing tools). Thus software is used, not generated (S2). The paper clearly generates substantial new research data: they measured 3147 new spectroscopic host galaxy redshifts via an extensive observational follow-up campaign (Hectospec, APO, WIYN, AAT), created new SN light curves via reprocessing, added new CC SN templates to the SNANA library, and generated large sets of Monte Carlo simulations used as a central part of the analysis. This clearly constitutes generated research data (D1), including observational redshift survey data and simulation outputs created specifically for this work.

The study generated new experimental research data: blood samples, erythrocyte/leukocyte profiles, PBMC proliferation assays, ELISA immunoglobulin measurements, and PTPRC genotyping data from 30-35 cattle infested with ticks. This is clearly D1 (data generated) as they created new research data through experiments. For software, they used standard statistical tools (R, mgcv package, gam function) which are generic statistical/plotting software used as utilities for analysis rather than software developed as a research contribution - this falls under S3 (no research software claimed as a contribution, only used as analysis utility).

This is a purely conceptual/theoretical paper that reviews literature on bureaucracy and analyzes the Balanced Scorecard framework through a conceptual lens. It does not generate or use any research software, nor does it collect, generate, or analyze any research data (no empirical data, surveys, interviews, or datasets are used). The paper explicitly states it offers no empirical support and is based solely on literature review and conceptual analysis.

This is a review/survey paper summarizing literature on energy storage for renewable-energy-powered water desalination systems. It does not report development of any new software/tool, nor does it use or generate any research data of its own; it only discusses and synthesizes findings, figures, and results from previously published studies without performing new experiments, simulations, or data collection. Hence it falls under No Software, No Data (S3D3).

The paper applies existing ML tools (Weka, JADBio) plus a SANN model variant from prior work (used, not newly created as a contribution here) to analyze and generate new data: the 192-patient autism assessment dataset, and newly collected questionnaire response data (30 and 18 patients) for the novel ASTA screening tool. No new software/algorithm is claimed as a core contribution of this paper (SANN is cited from prior work [73]); existing ML software (Weka, JADBio) is used for analysis. However, new research data (survey responses, screening tool data) was generated/collected specifically for this study, fitting D1. Thus S2 (software used, not generated) and D1 (data generated).

The paper develops an EMS algorithm implemented using existing tools (MATLAB, LABVIEW, MILP solvers) rather than creating new standalone research software for distribution—this is S3 since software is used as a utility for simulation/control rather than being the research contribution itself. The paper generates substantial research data: simulated load/PV forecasting profiles using ANFIS trained on data, experimental measurements from the laboratory microgrid (actual power drawn, SOC curves, load/PV profiles), and synthetically created PV generation forecasts with injected MAPE error. These are newly generated datasets from experiments and simulations, warranting D1.

The paper used only standard, generic software (SPSS, Matlab clustering, Adobe Audition) as utilities for data processing/editing rather than developing or extending research software, so it falls under S3 (no research software). The researchers collected original field recordings and conducted an experimental survey with 120 participants, generating new questionnaire data (SQE and LoW ratings) and audio/video soundscape samples, which constitutes newly generated research data (D1), also made available on Mendeley Data.

The study generated original behavioral observation data (ethogram-based activity budgets from CCTV monitoring of binturong) during zoo open/closed conditions, which qualifies as newly generated research data (D1). The paper uses R for statistical analysis, but this is a generic statistical software tool (treated as not research software), and no custom software/code was developed or claimed as a contribution, so this falls under S3 (No Research Software).

This is a post-hoc analysis of trial data from the SSaSS cluster randomised controlled trial. The paper uses pre-existing (previously collected) data from the trial to analyze cancer outcomes, which constitutes research data used (D2) rather than newly generated for this specific analysis. The data was collected during the original trial and is being reused/re-analyzed here. For software, the paper only mentions use of SAS software, a generic statistical software package, for analysis - this is explicitly listed as not research software under the criteria (generic statistical software). No research software was developed or claimed as a contribution, so this is S3 (No Research Software).

The paper generates original research data: EEG-fMRI recordings from 10 patients, IED-related BOLD maps, DCM effective connectivity results, and SEEG/surgical outcome data collected and analyzed specifically for this study - clearly D1 (data generated). Regarding software, the authors use established neuroimaging tools (SPM12/DCM10 module, FreeSurfer, FSL/FLIRT, 3D Slicer, ICN_Atlas, SEEGA) but do not claim to have created or significantly extended any of these tools themselves - they applied existing research software packages for preprocessing, analysis, and visualization. This is S2 (software used) rather than S1, since there's no claim of developing new software or algorithms, only applying an existing analytic framework (DCM) to a new clinical population.

This is a narrative review article that discusses and synthesizes findings from previously published GWAS and Mendelian randomisation studies on the link between type 2 diabetes and cancer. It does not generate or use any specific research software (no code, tools, or pipelines are developed or applied by the authors), and it does not generate or analyze any new research data itself—it only cites and discusses results/statistics from other published studies. As a review/opinion piece without original data or software use, it falls into S3D3.

The paper develops a conceptual process-optimization model (not software code/implementation) and validates it through two real-world case studies (automobile and mining machinery assembly shop floors). The production data (lead times, uptime, ergonomics issues, environmental factors) collected and tabulated in these case studies represent newly generated research data from observations/fieldwork. No research software was created or used—the 'model' is a management methodology/workflow, not source code or an algorithmic implementation, so it falls under 'No Software'. Data generated through case study observation and measurement qualifies as D1.

The paper uses existing household panel survey data (Russia Longitudinal Monitoring Survey, RLMS) collected by others, not newly generated by the authors - this is D2 (data used). The authors use standard econometric software/methods (fixed-effects regressions, ordered logit BUC estimator from Baetschmann et al. 2020) but do not claim to have created or significantly extended any research software themselves; they use an existing Stata command (feologit) for estimation. This qualifies as S2 (software used, not generated).

This is a purely theoretical linear algebra paper proving mathematical theorems about matrix symmetry decompositions and pseudoinverses. It uses a small numerical example (the Wilson matrix) to illustrate the theory, but this is a standard test matrix rather than research data collected/generated, and the paper does not create or use any research software (calculations appear to be done analytically/manually, not via any claimed software contribution). The data availability statement explicitly states "No data was used for the research described in the article." No software package, tool, or code is described as created or used as a research contribution.

The paper uses an existing numerical model/code (described in Willis et al. 2007, "available on request"), which they employ to run a suite of simulations but do not claim to have created or significantly extended the software itself - it's described as pre-existing code used for the simulations (S2). However, the paper generates substantial new research data through its extensive suite of 68+ numerical simulations of rotating convection with CMB heat flux heterogeneity - this simulation output data (temperature fields, velocity fields, etc.) is newly generated research data for this study, making it D1. The simulations explore new parameter regimes (lower Ekman numbers, higher Rayleigh numbers) not previously investigated, and the paper states data is "available from the corresponding author on request" confirming it was generated as part of this research.

The paper uses existing public sequencing data (NABEC long-read WGS dataset, 222 samples) to analyze HERV-K structural variants - this is data use (D2) from a pre-existing publicly available dataset. They also derive new findings/statistics and characterize novel insertion sequences, but these are findings derived from existing data rather than newly generated primary research data. For software, they use existing established bioinformatics tools (Sniffles2, EMBOSS, FASTA, BLAST, RepeatMasker, MAFFT, IQ-TREE2, RIdeogram, Plotrix, Napu pipeline) without claiming to create or significantly extend any of them - this is clear software use (S2), not generation.

The paper uses existing surveillance/traveler data (WHO case reports, traveler volume statistics, trip length estimates) to derive statistical estimates of MERS cases, qualifying as D2 (data used, with findings derived from data sources). No new research software is created; calculations use a formula/profile-likelihood method described analytically, not a software tool claimed as a contribution, so it is S3 (no software).

This paper involves field collection of sharks and copepod specimens, histological preparation and examination generating new observational/histopathology data (images, descriptions of infection pathology) - this constitutes generated research data. No research software is created or used as a contribution; only standard lab equipment (autostainer) and standard processing are mentioned, not computational software. Hence S3 (no research software) and D1 (data generated through original histological specimen collection and analysis).

The paper generates substantial new research data: 44 new phage isolates with sequenced genomes, metagenomic sequencing data, TEM images, viral/bacterial abundance counts, 16S rRNA sequences, and genome annotations deposited at NCBI/DSMZ - clearly D1 (data generated). For software, the authors use multiple existing bioinformatics tools (SPAdes, Tadpole, Bandage, PhageTerm, VirClust, ViPTree, VICTOR, GRAViTy, VIRIDIC, MUSCLE, IQ-Tree, BLAST, WIsH, CRISPRCasFinder, ARB, RAxML, MiGA, FigTree) but there is no claim of creating or significantly extending any software tool - these are all used as utilities for analysis, classifying as S2 (software used).

The paper uses existing general-purpose statistical software (R, with 'optim', 'NumDeriv', and 'ltm' packages) to implement the estimation and test computations, but does not claim to have developed new research software - these are utility tools for optimization/numerical derivatives, not a contribution in themselves, falling under S2 (or arguably S3, but R packages used are generic statistical tools so this is borderline S2/S3; since 'ltm' is a research-specific IRT package used as a tool, we classify as S2 Used). The paper generates extensive simulated data (Monte Carlo simulation study generating data under various misspecification scenarios) which constitutes generated research data (D1), and also analyzes a real dataset (Detroit Area Study), which is used but the simulation data generation is the primary data generation activity, placing this in D1.

The paper describes the creation of a novel online software tool, the Cool Farm Biodiversity metric, which constitutes significant research software development (S1). The authors also generated original research data through structured expert elicitation (expert judgement and evidence assessment scores for actions/species groups across biomes), compiled into new scoring datasets (provided in Supplementary Table S12), and collected/analyzed farm-level output data (e.g., example farm before/after scores). This qualifies as generated research data (D1), since the underlying scores, species group assessments, and farm case study data were created specifically for this research.

The paper is an experimental pharmaceutics study generating new data via DSC, PXRD, FTIR, and dissolution experiments on synthesized solid dispersions. Software mentioned (EVA, TA universal analysis, OMNIC) are generic instrument/analysis utility software, not research software created or significantly extended by the authors, so S3. The study clearly generates new experimental research data (crystallinity measurements, spectra, dissolution profiles), fitting D1.

This is a historical/architectural history humanities paper based on archival research (letters, exhibition catalogues, newspapers, RIBA archives). It does not involve creation or use of research software, nor does it generate or use research data in the sense defined (e.g., datasets, measurements, etc.). The archival/documentary sources consulted (letters, catalogues) are primary historical sources/literature rather than research data as defined by the criteria, and no software is used or created. Hence it falls into S3D3.

This is a scoping review that systematically searched databases and synthesized findings from seven included clinical trials on fluoride mouthwashes' effects on orthodontic appliances. The authors used standard tools (RoB2, ROBINS-I) for risk of bias assessment and Excel/EndNote as generic utility software, not as research software contributions - so S3. The paper uses existing research data in the form of the data extracted from the included studies (their results, measurements, risk of bias assessments) which were synthesized into tables - this constitutes using existing research data (findings/statistics derived from data sources from the included primary studies), classifying as D2. No new experimental/primary data was generated by this review itself.

This is a crystal structure report (IUCrData) describing a newly synthesized compound characterized by X-ray diffraction. The crystallographic data (atomic coordinates, bond lengths/angles, hydrogen-bond geometry, displacement parameters) were generated by the research itself, constituting newly created research data (D1). The software used (APEX3, SAINT, SADABS, SHELXT, SHELXL, DIAMOND) are established crystallographic software packages employed for structure solution/refinement/visualization, but are not claimed to have been created or extended by the authors - they are pre-existing research software tools used to produce the results (S2).

The paper reports an evaluation study where the authors conducted focus groups and interviews with 22 teachers, generating interview transcripts and survey data (research data generated). They used NVivo, a generic qualitative data analysis software package, purely as a utility for coding and clustering themes, not as a research contribution in itself - this falls under S3 (software used only as a utility, not claimed as a research contribution). No research software was created or significantly extended. Since new data (interview transcripts, focus group recordings, survey responses) was collected and generated specifically for this research, this qualifies as D1 (Data Generated).

This is a literature review article that synthesizes and summarizes findings from numerous other published studies on protein-ionic liquid interactions. The authors did not generate any new research software, nor did they use existing research software as part of a methodology (any mention of software like COSMO-RS is in the context of describing cited studies, not the authors' own use). Similarly, the paper does not report generation of new research data (e.g., new experiments, new datasets) nor direct use/analysis of a specific existing research dataset by the authors themselves - instead it compiles and discusses data and findings reported in many other primary research papers into summary tables for review purposes. As a review/survey paper without original experimental work, software development, or direct dataset analysis by the authors, it falls into the No Software, No Data category.

This is a qualitative single-case study using interviews (25 personal interviews), non-participant observations, document and archival research, and secondary data (press releases, media) collected over a longitudinal fieldwork period (2007-2014). This constitutes research data generation (interview transcripts, observational notes, archival material compiled for research purposes). There is no mention of any research software being created or used (no analysis software, statistical tools, or computational methods mentioned - only interpretive content analysis conducted manually). Thus the paper falls under No Software, Data Generated.

The paper is an experimental physics study generating original research data (PL spectra, g2(τ) measurements, ODMR spectra, magnetic field dependence data) from hBN defect samples - this is clearly newly generated research data (D1), with a data availability statement confirming data was generated ('available from corresponding authors upon reasonable request'). Regarding software, the paper mentions a 'code availability' statement for analysis code, but there is no claim that they developed or significantly extended novel research software - the code appears to be standard analysis/fitting scripts (e.g., for exponential fits, Lorentzian fits) used as a utility for processing their data rather than a novel software contribution. No specific named software package or tool is described as being created or substantially extended as a research contribution in itself, so this falls under S3 (software used only as utility, not a core contribution).
